history.heading: Early history
paragraphs: Cameroon has been inhabited since ancient times; the region is thought to be the homeland from which Bantu-speaking peoples began migrating across central and southern Africa thousands of years ago. Kingdoms and states developed, such as the Sao civilisation near Lake Chad, the Kotoko states, the Bamum kingdom with its own script invented by King Njoya, and Fulani emirates in the north.
Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, "river of prawns", which gave the country its name.

history.heading: Colonial rule
paragraphs: Germany established the colony of Kamerun in 1884. After the First World War the territory was divided between France and Britain as League of Nations mandates, with France governing the larger eastern part and Britain administering two western regions attached to Nigeria.
An armed struggle for independence led by the Union of the Peoples of Cameroon (UPC) was brutally suppressed by French forces in the 1950s and 1960s.

history.heading: Independence and unification
paragraphs: French Cameroon became independent on 1 January 1960. In 1961 the southern part of British Cameroons voted to join it, while the northern part joined Nigeria. Ahmadou Ahidjo ruled until 1982, and Paul Biya has been president since then, one of the longest-serving leaders in the world.

Since 2016 the English-speaking regions have experienced a conflict between separatists and government forces, known as the Anglophone crisis, which has killed thousands. The north has suffered attacks by Boko Haram.

culture.heading: "Africa in miniature"
paragraphs: Cameroon is often called "Africa in miniature" because of its great diversity of landscapes, from rainforest and mountains to savanna, and its more than 250 ethnic groups and languages. French and English are both official languages.

Christianity is predominant in the south and Islam in the north, with traditional beliefs throughout. Music styles such as makossa (with Manu Dibango, famous for Soul Makossa) and bikutsi are popular across Africa.

culture.heading: Food and football
paragraphs: Ndolé, a stew of bitter leaves with peanuts and meat or fish, is considered the national dish, along with fufu, plantains and grilled fish. Football is a passion; the Indomitable Lions reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1990, and Samuel Eto'o and Roger Milla are national heroes.

politics.heading: Strong presidency
paragraphs: Cameroon is a presidential republic in which the president holds extensive powers. Paul Biya's party, the Cameroon People's Democratic Movement, dominates parliament. Term limits were removed in 2008, and elections have been criticised as neither free nor fair; Biya was declared winner of a further term in 2025 amid opposition protests.
Key issues include the Anglophone conflict, security in the Far North and the eventual succession of the ageing president.

economy.heading: A diversified economy
paragraphs: Cameroon has one of the more diversified economies in Central Africa. It exports oil, timber, cocoa, coffee, cotton, bananas and aluminium. The port of Douala is a gateway for landlocked Chad and the Central African Republic.
Cameroon uses the Central African CFA franc. Despite its resources, poverty remains high, especially in the north, and corruption and conflict hamper development.
